title: EC2 Troubleshooting
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of ec2 troubleshooting and its relationship to Amazon EC2 and Virtual Servers.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to ec2 troubleshooting.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn ec2 troubleshooting in the context of Amazon EC2 and Virtual Servers. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: EC2 Troubleshooting matters because it is one part of amazon ec2 and virtual servers. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: Module 6: Amazon EC2 and Virtual Servers
content_blocks.alt_text: Five-step overview for module 6, Amazon EC2 and Virtual Servers, followed by verification, least-privilege security, recovery, and cost-cleanup checks.
content_blocks.caption: Module 6 learning sequence: understand the concept, make a controlled design/configuration, verify behavior, and document security/reliability/cost trade-offs.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** EC2 Troubleshooting belongs to Amazon EC2 and Virtual Servers. EC2 is a flexible virtual-server option. Safe operation includes image hygiene, least-privilege instance roles, patching, persistent-storage awareness, monitoring and cleanup.

The PDF lists these subtopics: Failed instance launches; SSH and connectivity failures; Boot and status-check failures; Storage, CPU, and memory troubleshooting. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For ec2 troubleshooting, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: Failed instance launches
items.text: Define the input/data permissions, expected evidence, evaluation cases, safety boundaries and cost limits. A generated answer or completed invocation is not by itself proof of correctness.

items.title: SSH and connectivity failures
items.text: Trace the path from source to destination through address ranges, routing, gateways and filtering controls. Verify both forward and return paths; one successful configuration screen is not proof of reachability.

items.title: Boot and status-check failures
items.text: Define the failure scenario and recovery objective, then test detection, recovery, data consistency and rollback. Treat recovery evidence as a deliverable, not an assumption.

items.title: Storage, CPU, and memory troubleshooting
items.text: Select a signal tied to the user-visible symptom, identify its source and time window, and make the response actionable through an owner, threshold and runbook.

content_blocks.title: Instance lifecycle: EC2 Troubleshooting
content_blocks.code:
pending → running → stopping → stopped
running → shutting-down → terminated
A stopped instance can retain EBS volumes and other resources.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “EC2 Troubleshooting”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. Do not create or alter billable resources unless the account owner has approved the lab.
hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for EC2 Troubleshooting with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: EC2 Troubleshooting is taught as part of Amazon EC2 and Virtual Servers.
EC2 is a flexible virtual-server option. Safe operation includes image hygiene, least-privilege instance roles, patching, persistent-storage awareness, monitoring and cleanup.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
